claim: The last common ancestor of percomorphs (including medaka and cichlids) and ostariophysi (including zebrafish) lived approximately 240 million years ago.
source: Medaka and cichlids belong to a diverse clade of teleosts known as percomorphs, whose last common ancestor with ostariophysi, such as zebrafish and Mexican cavefish, lived ~240 mya (Betancur-R et al., 2017; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Betancur-R et al., 2017, which provides the phylogenetic timing estimate.

claim: Medaka and cichlids diverged approximately 100 million years ago.
source: While medaka and cichlids are only distantly related (~100 mya; Betancur-R et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Betancur-R et al., 2017, which provides the phylogenetic timing estimate.

claim: The haplochromine and lamprologine cichlid species studied diverged within the past 3 million years.
source: the haplochromine species and the three lamprologine species studied here diverged recently, within the past 3 million years (Ronco et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ronco et al., 2021, which provides the phylogenetic timing estimate.

claim: Zebrafish larvae at 5-7 days post-fertilization robustly feed on small prey items such as paramecia.
source: At 5–7 days post-fertilization (dpf), zebrafish larvae robustly feed on small prey items such as paramecia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about zebrafish larval feeding behavior.

claim: Juvenile zebrafish feed on zooplankton such as brine shrimp (artemia), which are too large for larvae to ingest.
source: As juveniles, they feed on zooplankton such as brine shrimp (artemia), which are too large for larvae to ingest.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about zebrafish feeding behavior at different developmental stages.

claim: Cichlid larvae started feeding later than zebrafish, from 12 to 14 days post-fertilization.
source: Cichlid larvae started feeding later than zebrafish, from 12 to 14 dpf
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data collected in this study.

claim: Medaka (OL) started feeding at approximately 10 days post-fertilization.
source: medaka (OL) started feeding at approximately 10 dpf.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data collected in this study.

claim: Medaka (OL) and A. burtoni (AB) swim with a continuous 'gliding' style characterized by sustained, uninterrupted tail undulations over many seconds with only short breaks between swimming episodes.
source: On one extreme, medaka (OL) and A. burtoni (AB) swam with a continuous 'gliding' style characterized by sustained, uninterrupted tail undulations over many seconds with only short breaks between swimming episodes, similar to Danionella.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings.

claim: L. ocellatus (LO) and N. multifasciatus (NM) have an intermittent swimming style, often resting at the bottom of the chamber for minutes at a time with quiescent periods interrupted by short, rapid bursts of activity.
source: On the other extreme, L. ocellatus (LO) and N. multifasciatus (NM) had an intermittent swimming style, often resting at the bottom of the chamber for minutes at a time with quiescent periods interrupted by short, rapid bursts of activity.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings.

claim: L. attenuatus (LA) shows a behavior intermediate between continuous gliding and intermittent swimming, alternating between rapid tail beating and quiescence, each lasting on the order of a few seconds.
source: L. attenuatus (LA) showed a behavior intermediate to these extremes, alternating between rapid tail beating and quiescence, each lasting on the order of a few seconds, a discontinuous style similar to zebrafish.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings.

claim: Medaka (OL) exhibited considerably longer behavioral syllables than cichlids (p<0.01).
source: Furthermore, medaka (OL) exhibited considerably longer syllables than cichlids (p<0.01, bootstrap test difference between medians)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: N. multifasciatus (NM) exhibited significantly shorter behavioral syllables than other cichlid species (p<0.05).
source: while one cichlid species, NM, exhibited significantly shorter syllables than the others (p<0.05) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Zebrafish larvae converge their eyes (nasalward rotation) at the onset of hunting episodes and keep their eyes converged over the course of prey capture.
source: Zebrafish larvae converge their eyes (nasalward rotation, Figure 2A) at the onset of hunting episodes and keep their eyes converged over the course of prey capture (Bianco et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on zebrafish prey capture behavior.

claim: Eye convergence aids prey capture in zebrafish by bringing prey into a binocular zone in the central visual field.
source: Eye convergence aids prey capture by bringing prey into a binocular zone in the central visual field (Gahtan et al., 2005; Gebhardt et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on zebrafish visual behavior during prey capture.

claim: All four cichlid species examined converge their eyes during prey capture.
source: We found that all four cichlid species examined here converged their eyes during prey capture, but medaka did not (Figure 3A; Figure 1—video 2 through Figure 1—video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, supported by Figure 3A and video recordings.

claim: Medaka do not converge their eyes during prey capture.
source: We found that all four cichlid species examined here converged their eyes during prey capture, but medaka did not (Figure 3A; Figure 1—video 2 through Figure 1—video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, supported by Figure 3A and video recordings.

claim: For all cichlid species except medaka (OL), modeling eye convergence data using two underlying distributions provided a better fit than a single distribution.
source: For all species except OL, modeling the data using two underlying distributions provided a better fit than a single distribution (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling (Gaussian mixture models) of the experimental data, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: L. attenuatus (LA) spent about a quarter of the time actively engaged in prey capture (median: 0.25).
source: In contrast, LA, a piscivorous species as adults, spent about a quarter of the time actively engaged in prey capture, with all individuals tested spending at least 10% of their time and one individual spending over 40% of the time hunting (median: 0.25, p-values<0.05 comparing LA to all other species, Mann-Whitney U test with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: L. ocellatus (LO), N. multifasciatus (NM), and A. burtoni (AB) spent less than 10% of the time hunting.
source: LO, NM, and AB spent less than 10% of the time hunting (median proportions: 0.064, LO; 0.036, NM; 0.096, AB).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A. burtoni (AB) initiated hunts at a much higher rate than L. ocellatus (LO) and N. multifasciatus (NM), similar to L. attenuatus (LA).
source: Surprisingly, although LO, NM, and AB all spent comparable total time engaged in prey capture, AB initiated hunts at a much higher rate, similar to LA (Figure 3D) (median hunts/min: 2.45, LO; 1.98, NM; 6.85, LA; 8.49, AB; p-values<0.05 comparing either LO or NM to LA or AB, Mann-Whitney U test with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A. burtoni (AB) hunts were shorter than other cichlid species.
source: AB hunts were also shorter than other species, while LA hunts tended to be longer (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: L. attenuatus (LA) hunts tended to be longer than other cichlid species.
source: AB hunts were also shorter than other species, while LA hunts tended to be longer (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: All three cichlid species (LO, NM, LA) consumed prey at similar rates of approximately one artemia per minute.
source: Despite these differences in time engaged in prey capture, all three species consumed prey at similar rates of approximately one artemia per minute (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Zebrafish larvae strike at prey once it is localized in the center of their visual field and approximately 0.5 mm away (the 'strike zone').
source: Zebrafish larvae strike at prey once it is localized in the center of their visual field and ~0.5 mm away (the 'strike zone') (Mearns et al., 2020; Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on zebrafish prey capture behavior.

claim: Within each prey capture sequence, prey became increasingly localized to the near-central visual field over time in cichlids.
source: This revealed that, within each prey capture sequence, prey became increasingly localized to the near-central visual field over time.
evidence: This is based on analysis of prey trajectories during hunting episodes, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cichlids initiate prey capture at a wide range of distances.
source: Computing kernel density estimates of prey distributions at the beginning, middle, and end of each hunting episode revealed that cichlids initiate prey capture at a wide range of distances, and that they center prey in the visual field in the early stages of a hunting sequence (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of prey distributions during hunting episodes, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cichlids center prey in the visual field in the early stages of a hunting sequence.
source: Computing kernel density estimates of prey distributions at the beginning, middle, and end of each hunting episode revealed that cichlids initiate prey capture at a wide range of distances, and that they center prey in the visual field in the early stages of a hunting sequence (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of prey distributions during hunting episodes, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The azimuthal angle of prey decreased over the start of the hunting episode in L. ocellatus (LO) and N. multifasciatus (NM) (p<0.01).
source: For instance, the azimuthal angle of prey decreased over the start of the hunting episode in LO and NM (p<0.01, bootstrap test difference between medians) (Figure 4D), but not over the second half (p>0.05).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of prey positioning data during hunting episodes, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: On average, the cichlids' eyes converged when prey were approximately 5 mm away.
source: On average, the cichlids' eyes converged when prey were ~5 mm away (median distance, mm: 5.43, LO; 3.98, NM; 4.17, LA).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of prey distance at the onset of eye convergence.

claim: All cichlid species could detect prey up to 15 mm away.
source: However, all species could detect prey up to 15 mm away (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of prey detection distances, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In all cichlid species analyzed, prey were highly localized to a central strike zone approximately 1-2 mm away at the end of prey capture.
source: In all cichlid species analyzed, prey were highly localized to a central strike zone ~1–2 mm away at the end of prey capture (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of prey positioning at the end of hunting episodes, shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Tail pose dynamics are similarly low-dimensional across all species studied, with three principal components explaining >90% variance.
source: Performing principal components analysis (PCA) on all species combined revealed that tail pose dynamics are similarly low-dimensional (Figure 5A, black line; three principal components [PCs] explain >90% variance). These results also hold when each species is analyzed individually (Figure 5A, colored lines).
evidence: This is based on principal components analysis of tail kinematics data, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The principal components of tail pose correspond to a harmonic series, with the first PC capturing 'turniness', and PCs 2 and 3 capturing tail oscillations during locomotion.
source: As with zebrafish larvae (Girdhar et al., 2015; Mearns et al., 2020), the PCs correspond to a harmonic series (Figure 5B), with the first PC capturing 'turniness', and PCs 2 and 3 capturing tail oscillations during locomotion.
evidence: This is based on analysis of principal components and comparison to previous zebrafish studies, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The first three principal components were similar across species.
source: The first three PCs were similar across species (Figure 5C), allowing swim kinematics to be compared across species.
evidence: This is based on comparison of principal components across species, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cichlids have behavioral syllables that they preferentially perform during prey capture.
source: Similar to zebrafish, we found that cichlids have behavioral syllables that they preferentially perform during prey capture (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of behavioral bouts and their association with prey capture, shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cichlid larvae often 'hover' in place, oscillating their tail without any forward movement.
source: For example, cichlid larvae often 'hover' in place, oscillating their tail without any forward movement (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings, shown in Figure 5G.

claim: During hunting, cichlids will alternate between approaches and hover swims.
source: During hunting, cichlids will alternate between approaches and these hover swims.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings.

claim: During tail coiling in cichlids, the tail coils into an S-shape over many hundreds of milliseconds leading up to a strike, and the coil is released rapidly during the strike, allowing fish to spring toward the prey.
source: Another feature of cichlid hunting behavior not present in zebrafish is tail coiling. Here, the tail coils into an S-shape over many hundreds of milliseconds leading up to a strike. The coil is released rapidly during the strike, allowing fish to spring toward the prey (Figure 5G, bottom center; Figure 4I; Figure 1—video 2, 00:12; Figure 1—video 4, 00:31).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings, shown in Figure 5G and videos.

claim: Cichlids exhibit a range of poststrike maneuvers not present in zebrafish, including expelling prey ('spitting') and swimming backward to re-center prey.
source: Finally, we found that cichlids exhibit a range of poststrike maneuvers not present in zebrafish. These include expelling prey ('spitting') that has already been captured (Figure 5—video 1) and swimming backward to re-center prey in the visual field in cases where capture strikes miss (Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings.

claim: Spitting behavior often triggered another attempt to hunt and capture the same prey and was particularly common in L. attenuatus (LA).
source: Spitting behavior often triggered another attempt to hunt and capture the same prey and was particularly common in LA.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings.

claim: Cichlid captures often occur in two phases, with the prey first being caught by the pharyngeal jaws before being ingested.
source: We also find that cichlid captures often occur in two phases, with the prey first being caught by the pharyngeal jaws (a second, internal set of jaws present in cichlids; Liem, 1973) before being ingested.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, with reference to the anatomical feature (pharyngeal jaws) cited from Liem, 1973.

claim: Medaka (OL) did not strike at prey in the central visual field but rather captured prey in the lateral visual field with a side-swing behavior.
source: Remarkably, we found that OL did not strike at prey in the central visual but rather captured prey in the lateral visual field with a side-swing behavior (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data and video recordings, shown in Figures 5H-J.

claim: Strikes from all cichlid species were similar to each other, while the side-swing strike was highly enriched in medaka (OL).
source: We found that strikes from all cichlid species were similar to each other, while the side-swing strike was highly enriched in OL (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of capture strikes across species, shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Cichlids have at least two kinematically distinct capture strikes: a slower behavior similar to the zebrafish attack swim and a faster capture spring.
source: This analysis uncovered at least two kinematically distinct capture strikes in cichlids. The slower of these behaviors is similar to the zebrafish attack swim, characterized by a symmetric undulation of the tail about the midline which propels the fish toward the prey, while the faster corresponds to the capture spring.
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of capture strikes and comparison to zebrafish behavior, shown in Figure 5K and 5L.

claim: The rate of change in heading was greater in medaka than in L. attenuatus (LA) leading up to a strike (p<0.001).
source: We found that the rate of change in heading was greater in medaka than in cichlids (median °/s: –13.4, LA; –34.1, OL; p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of heading changes during prey approach, shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Cichlids share the same general hunting strategy as zebrafish: striking at prey localized to a binocular strike zone while the eyes are converged.
source: We have found that cichlids share the same general hunting strategy to zebrafish: striking at prey localized to a binocular strike zone while the eyes are converged, with two distinct capture bout types whose kinematics are remarkably similar given these species diverged 240 mya (see Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Medaka deploy a different hunting strategy than cichlids and zebrafish: striking at prey laterally in the monocular visual field with a side-swing behavior.
source: In contrast, medaka, which are phylogenetically intermediate to zebrafish and cichlids, deploy a different hunting strategy: striking at prey laterally in the monocular visual field with a side-swing behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The results are consistent with cichlids using binocular cues, such as binocular disparity, to determine distance to prey.
source: These results are consistent with cichlids using binocular cues, such as binocular disparity, to determine distance to prey, while medaka may employ a monocular strategy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of heading changes and prey positioning during hunting.

claim: Medaka may employ a monocular strategy to determine distance to prey.
source: These results are consistent with cichlids using binocular cues, such as binocular disparity, to determine distance to prey, while medaka may employ a monocular strategy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of heading changes and prey positioning during hunting.

claim: The hunting behavior of larval zebrafish (Danio rerio) has been well characterized.
source: The hunting behavior of larval zebrafish (Danio rerio), a cyprinid native to streams in Eastern India, has been well characterized.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: It is unknown if the complement and sequence of movements employed during prey capture by zebrafish is universal across freshwater teleosts.
source: However, it is unknown if the complement and sequence of movements employed during prey capture by zebrafish is universal across freshwater teleosts.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The repertoire of hunting movements of cichlids is broader than that of zebrafish.
source: Notably, we found that the repertoire of hunting movements of cichlids is broader than that of zebrafish, but shares basic features, such as eye convergence, positioning of prey centrally in the binocular visual field, and discrete prey capture bouts, including two kinds of capture strikes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data and behavioral analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cichlids and zebrafish share basic hunting features, such as eye convergence, positioning of prey centrally in the binocular visual field, and discrete prey capture bouts, including two kinds of capture strikes.
source: Notably, we found that the repertoire of hunting movements of cichlids is broader than that of zebrafish, but shares basic features, such as eye convergence, positioning of prey centrally in the binocular visual field, and discrete prey capture bouts, including two kinds of capture strikes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data and behavioral analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Medaka swim continuously, track the prey monocularly without eye convergence, and position prey laterally before capturing them with a side swing.
source: In contrast, medaka swim continuously, track the prey monocularly without eye convergence, and position prey laterally before capturing them with a side swing.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data and behavioral analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Medaka may judge distance to prey predominantly by motion parallax, while cichlids and zebrafish may mainly use binocular visual cues.
source: This configuration of kinematic motifs suggests that medaka may judge distance to prey predominantly by motion parallax, while cichlids and zebrafish may mainly use binocular visual cues.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences in hunting behavior and prey positioning strategies.

claim: Recent comparative behavioral studies in drosophilids that diverged less than 40 million years ago found differences in both locomotion and sequencing of spontaneous behaviors.
source: For example, recent comparative behavioral studies in drosophilids that diverged less than 40 mya found differences in both locomotion (York et al., 2022) and sequencing of spontaneous behaviors (Hernández et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to York et al., 2022 and Hernández et al., 2021.

claim: The zebrafish larva has become a dominant model for understanding the neuronal circuits and pathways controlling innate behavior.
source: For vertebrates, the zebrafish larva has become a dominant model for understanding the neuronal circuits and pathways controlling innate behavior (Baier and Scott, 2009; Friedrich et al., 2010; Gahtan and Baier, 2004; Orger and de Polavieja, 2017; Portugues and Engert, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on zebrafish neurobiology and behavior.

claim: Many aspects of the visuomotor transformations and underlying neural circuitry for prey capture have been revealed in zebrafish.
source: While many aspects of the visuomotor transformations and underlying neural circuitry for prey capture have been revealed in this species (reviewed by Baier and Scott, 2024; Zhu and Goodhill, 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on zebrafish prey capture neurobiology.

claim: It is not known if the zebrafish prey capture mechanism is the general solution for larval teleosts or a derived adaptation to the zebrafish's specific ecological niche.
source: it is not known if this is the general solution for larval teleosts or a derived adaptation to the zebrafish's specific ecological niche.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: At the week-old stage, zebrafish attack swims are the most common capture maneuver.
source: At the week-old stage, attack swims are the most common capture maneuver and consist of a symmetric oscillation of the tail that resembles spontaneous forward swims.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about zebrafish prey capture behavior.

claim: During a zebrafish S-strike, the tail does not oscillate, but rather bends into an S-shape and then straightens rapidly, causing larvae to lunge toward prey.
source: During an S-strike, the tail does not oscillate, but rather bends into an S-shape and then straightens rapidly, causing larvae to lunge toward prey.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about zebrafish prey capture behavior.

claim: Zebrafish attack swims and S-strikes are deployed variably, dependent on experience and different prey distances.
source: These strikes are deployed variably, dependent on experience and different prey distances (Lagogiannis et al., 2020; McClenahan et al., 2012; Mearns et al., 2020; Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on zebrafish prey capture behavior.

claim: At the first-feeding stage, zebrafish larvae swim in discrete, discontinuous bouts.
source: At the first-feeding stage, zebrafish larvae swim in discrete, discontinuous bouts (Budick and O'Malley, 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Budick and O'Malley, 2000.

claim: Zebrafish discrete swimming bouts merge into continuous swimming at the juvenile stage.
source: which merge into continuous swimming at the juvenile stage (Westphal and O'Malley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Westphal and O'Malley, 2013.

claim: Danionella cerebrum, a close relative of zebrafish, exhibits slow continuous swimming as larvae.
source: In contrast, Danionella cerebrum, a close relative of zebrafish, exhibits slow continuous swimming as larvae (Rajan et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rajan et al., 2022.

claim: Behavior is organized into sub-second kinematic motifs ('syllables'), even when movement is continuous.
source: Analyses across the animal kingdom suggest that behavior is organized into sub-second kinematic motifs ('syllables'), even when movement is continuous (Berman et al., 2014; Stephens et al., 2008; Tinbergen, 1951; Wiltschko et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies across different animal systems.

claim: Blind cave fish (Astyanax mexicanus) capture prey that are positioned laterally to their mouth.
source: In contrast, some fish species such as the blind cave fish, Astyanax mexicanus, capture prey that are positioned laterally to their mouth (Lloyd et al., 2018; Espinasa et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lloyd et al., 2018 and Espinasa et al., 2023.

claim: The shift in capture strategy in cavefish appears to have happened over a relatively short timescale when cavefish diverged from their surface ancestors.
source: This shift in capture strategy appears to have happened over a relatively short timescale when cavefish diverged from their surface ancestors
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies on cavefish evolution.

claim: Cavefish still converge their vestigial eyes even though they do not rely on vision for prey capture.
source: and consequently, cavefish still converge their vestigial eyes even though they do not rely on vision for prey capture (Espinasa and Lewis, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Espinasa and Lewis, 2023.

claim: Zebrafish centering behavior is impaired when animals are blinded in one eye.
source: This centering behavior is impaired when animals are blinded in one eye (Mearns et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mearns et al., 2020.

claim: L. attenuatus (LA) is a piscivorous species as adults.
source: In contrast, LA, a piscivorous species as adults, spent about a quarter of the time actively engaged in prey capture
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the species' adult feeding ecology.

claim: L. attenuatus (LA) are the most persistent hunters, initiating prey capture often and spending a longer time engaged in the behavior once initiated.
source: LA are the most persistent hunters, initiating prey capture often and spending a longer time engaged in the behavior once initiated (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the quantitative data presented in Figure 3.

claim: A. burtoni (AB) prey capture dynamics are characterized by a high rate of short-duration hunting episodes.
source: In contrast, AB prey capture dynamics are characterized by a high rate of short-duration hunting episodes (Figure 1—video 5).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the quantitative data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Both L. attenuatus (LA) and A. burtoni (AB) prey capture behaviors are examples of an active hunting strategy.
source: Both LA and AB prey capture behaviors are examples of an active hunting strategy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed hunting patterns and time spent hunting.

claim: L. ocellatus (LO) and N. multifasciatus (NM) initiate prey capture rarely, spending much time resting at the bottom of the chamber and moving only occasionally when they dart toward prey, characteristic of a sit-and-wait predation strategy.
source: On the other hand, LO and NM initiate prey capture rarely, spending much time resting at the bottom of the chamber and moving only occasionally when they dart toward prey (Figure 1—videos 3 and 4), characteristic of a sit-and-wait predation strategy.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the quantitative data and video observations.

claim: L. attenuatus (LA) often initiated prey capture when artemia were already in the center of the visual field.
source: Curiously, LA often initiated prey capture when artemia were already in the center of the visual field (Figure 4A, B, and D), which may be due to them restarting hunts on recently expelled prey (see description of spitting behavior below and Figure 1—video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, with a speculative explanation provided.

claim: The distance to the prey decreases gradually over the course of the hunting episode in cichlids.
source: However, all species could detect prey up to 15 mm away (Figure 4C), and the distance to the prey decreases gradually over the course of the hunting episode, in contrast to centering, which tends to occur at the beginning.
evidence: This is based on analysis of prey distance over time during hunting episodes, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Zebrafish larvae preferentially perform different kinds of swims during prey capture and exploration.
source: Zebrafish larvae preferentially perform different kinds of swims during prey capture and exploration (Borla et al., 2002; McElligott and O'Malley, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Borla et al., 2002 and McElligott and O'Malley, 2005.

claim: In zebrafish, different swim types mediate distinct transformations of the visual scene: J-turns center prey in the visual field, approach swims bring prey to the strike zone, and strikes are deployed to capture prey.
source: During prey capture, different swim types mediate distinct transformations of the visual scene: J-turns center prey in the visual field, approach swims bring prey to the strike zone, and strikes are deployed to capture prey.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about zebrafish prey capture behavior.

claim: The number of behavioral syllables identified ranged from 11 (LO) to 32 (AB) across cichlid species.
source: We also found notable diversity in the number of syllables across species, ranging from 11 (LO) to 32 (AB), which is on par with or greater than the bout types that have been found in zebrafish larvae (Marques et al., 2018; Mearns et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of behavioral bouts across species.

claim: Species with the most clusters identified (29 and 32 in LA and AB, respectively) performed more hunting sequences than LO or NM.
source: First, we note that species with the most clusters identified (29 and 32 in LA and AB, respectively) performed more hunting sequences than LO or NM (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on comparison of cluster numbers with hunting frequency data from Figure 3D.

claim: Hovering may aid in keeping animals in place during hunting by preventing them from being moved by convection currents or by breaking their forward momentum following more rapid forward swims.
source: We speculate that hovers may aid in keeping animals in place during hunting by preventing them from being moved by convection currents or by breaking their forward momentum following more rapid forward swims.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed hovering behavior.

claim: Hovering may allow animals to pause between sensorimotor decisions during hunting sequences while keeping the tail motile, reducing the latency of the motor system to respond to descending motor commands.
source: Alternatively, they may allow animals to pause between sensorimotor decisions during hunting sequences while keeping the tail motile, reducing the latency of the motor system to respond to descending motor commands.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed hovering behavior.

claim: Hovering is also present in some adult cichlids that use their lateral line to sense prey in the subsurface.
source: Interestingly, hovering is also present in some adult cichlids that use their lateral line to sense prey in the subsurface (Schwalbe et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwalbe et al., 2016.

claim: The S-shape of the tail leading up to the capture spring shares structural similarities with the S-strike of zebrafish larvae, differing primarily in the time course over which they occur.
source: The S-shape of the tail leading up to the capture spring shares structural similarities with the S-strike of zebrafish larvae (Mearns et al., 2020), differing primarily in the time course over which they occur.
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on the experimental data and comparison to zebrafish behavior.

claim: The S-strike of zebrafish may represent an accelerated form of the capture spring, forming and releasing over tens of milliseconds rather than hundreds of milliseconds seen in cichlids.
source: The S-strike of zebrafish may represent an accelerated form of the capture spring, forming and releasing over tens of milliseconds rather than hundreds of milliseconds seen in cichlids or, vice versa, the capture spring may represent an augmentation of the S-strike.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between zebrafish and cichlid capture strikes.

claim: The capture spring may represent an augmentation of the S-strike.
source: The S-strike of zebrafish may represent an accelerated form of the capture spring, forming and releasing over tens of milliseconds rather than hundreds of milliseconds seen in cichlids or, vice versa, the capture spring may represent an augmentation of the S-strike.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between zebrafish and cichlid capture strikes.

claim: Centralized prey and converged eyes in cichlids suggest that the mechanism they use to determine the distance to prey could be similar to that of zebrafish.
source: Centralized prey and converged eyes in cichlids suggest that the mechanism they use to determine the distance to prey could be similar to that of zebrafish. One possibility is that these species use binocular disparity to judge depth (Qian, 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed similarities in prey positioning and eye convergence, with a citation to a relevant mechanism.

claim: Medaka might use motion parallax to judge the distance to prey.
source: In contrast, we hypothesized that medaka (OL) might use a different, monocular strategy to judge the distance to prey, such as motion parallax (Yoonessi and Baker, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed differences in hunting behavior, with a citation to a relevant mechanism.

claim: Binocular disparity and motion parallax make different predictions about how larvae should approach prey to make best use of visual cues.
source: These two mechanisms of depth perception make different predictions about how larvae should approach prey to make best use of visual cues (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on known properties of these depth perception mechanisms, illustrated in Figure 5M.

claim: Medaka (OL) swimming is nearly continuous.
source: Medaka (OL) swimming is nearly continuous, and their eyes do not converge during prey capture.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Medaka (OL) may still perform different behaviors during spontaneous swimming and prey capture despite not converging their eyes.
source: Nevertheless, they may still perform different behaviors during spontaneous swimming and prey capture.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral clustering analysis.

claim: Medaka (OL) have a suite of behaviors similar to hunting bouts of cichlids and zebrafish, including J-turns, approach swims, and slow swims.
source: Investigating clusters of behavior in OL revealed types of swim that are similar to hunting bouts of cichlids and zebrafish. These included J-turns, approach swims, and slow swims (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of medaka behavioral bouts, shown in Figure 5H.

claim: There is sometimes a slight nasalward rotation of the ipsilateral eye in medaka leading up to and during the side swing.
source: Although the eyes do not converge, there is sometimes a slight nasalward rotation of the ipsilateral eye leading up to and during the side swing (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Adult cichlids are known to use their lateral line for prey capture.
source: Adult cichlids are known to use their lateral line for prey capture (Schwalbe et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwalbe et al., 2012.

claim: Some percomorph species exhibit both an S-strike-like and a sideways capture strategy as adults.
source: and some percomorph species exhibit both an S-strike-like and a sideways capture strategy as adults (New, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to New, 2002.

claim: Zebrafish larvae can still hunt in the dark, as do blind zebrafish lakritz mutants, albeit with greatly reduced efficacy, and with their eyes converged.
source: Zebrafish larvae can still hunt in the dark, as do blind zebrafish lakritz mutants, albeit with greatly reduced efficacy, and with their eyes converged (Gahtan et al., 2005; Mearns et al., 2020; Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gahtan et al., 2005, Mearns et al., 2020, and Patterson et al., 2013.

claim: Larval cavefish exhibit vestigial eye convergence movements during prey capture before their eyes fully degenerate.
source: Larval cavefish, which evolved from sighted surface ancestors and are completely blind, exhibit vestigial eye convergence movements during prey capture before their eyes fully degenerate (Espinasa et al., 2023; Espinasa and Lewis, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Espinasa et al., 2023 and Espinasa and Lewis, 2023.

claim: The teleost brain employs cues from both vision and lateral line sensory modalities, if available, to locate prey.
source: This comparative evidence suggests that the teleost brain employs cues from both sensory modalities, if available, to locate prey, but that eye movements are a poor predictor of the dominance of vision.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative evidence from multiple species.

claim: Eye movements are a poor predictor of the dominance of vision in teleost prey capture.
source: This comparative evidence suggests that the teleost brain employs cues from both sensory modalities, if available, to locate prey, but that eye movements are a poor predictor of the dominance of vision.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative evidence from multiple species.

claim: Zebrafish use binocular information and stationary differences such as brightness and contrast to estimate depth and distance.
source: Zebrafish use binocular information (Gahtan et al., 2005; Gebhardt et al., 2019; Henriques et al., 2019) and stationary differences such as brightness and contrast (Khan et al., 2023) to estimate depth and distance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on zebrafish depth perception.

claim: Cichlid larvae likely use binocular cues for distance estimation.
source: Here, we have shown that cichlid larvae also likely use binocular cues, while medaka's approach to prey conforms to a monocular strategy (see Figure 5M and N).
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of heading changes and prey positioning, shown in Figures 5M and 5N.

claim: Medaka's approach to prey conforms to a monocular strategy.
source: Here, we have shown that cichlid larvae also likely use binocular cues, while medaka's approach to prey conforms to a monocular strategy (see Figure 5M and N).
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of heading changes and prey positioning, shown in Figures 5M and 5N.

claim: Cichlid and zebrafish larvae swim in bouts with intermittent pauses, while medaka swim continuously with longer bouts ('gliding').
source: Strikingly, cichlid and zebrafish larvae swim in bouts with intermittent pauses, while medaka swim continuously with longer bouts ('gliding').
evidence: This is a summary of the swimming pattern observations from the experimental data.

claim: The pauses in cichlid and zebrafish swimming may serve to sample the distance to the prey by comparing its position across the two eyes.
source: We speculate that the pauses may serve to sample the distance to the prey by comparing its position across the two eyes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed swimming patterns.

claim: To sample motion cues, it is advantageous to perform continuous glides and swim lateral to the prey up until it is close enough for a sideways strike.
source: In contrast, to sample motion cues, it is advantageous to perform continuous glides and swim lateral to the prey up until it is close enough for a sideways strike.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed swimming patterns in medaka.

claim: Natural selection may have favored specific locomotor (bouts vs. glides) and oculomotor (convergent vs. divergent) adaptations of behavioral control depending on the dominant distance measurement mechanism (binocular vs. monocular).
source: Thus, natural selection may have favored specific locomotor (bouts vs. glides) and oculomotor (convergent vs. divergent) adaptations of behavioral control depending on the dominant distance measurement mechanism (binocular vs. monocular) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation of the observed behavioral differences.

claim: Cichlids and medaka may also use size, brightness, and contrast cues to estimate prey distance in addition to binocular disparity and monocular parallax mechanisms.
source: Cichlids and medaka may also use size, brightness, and contrast cues to estimate prey distance in addition to the binocular disparity and monocular parallax mechanisms we have postulated here.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about additional possible mechanisms for distance estimation.

claim: Eye convergence is not always a hallmark of prey capture in fish larvae.
source: We have demonstrated that eye convergence is not always a hallmark of prey capture in fish larvae, and that multiple, kinematically distinct capture swims exist at these early stages in different species.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data showing medaka do not converge their eyes.

claim: Multiple, kinematically distinct capture swims exist at early larval stages in different fish species.
source: We have demonstrated that eye convergence is not always a hallmark of prey capture in fish larvae, and that multiple, kinematically distinct capture swims exist at these early stages in different species.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data showing different capture strike types.

claim: Ocular vergence angles and swim kinematics for prey capture might coevolve, with S-strike-like captures and attack swims being associated with convergent eyes and side-swing captures occurring in the absence of eye convergence.
source: We speculate that ocular vergence angles and swim kinematics for prey capture might coevolve, with S-strike-like captures and attack swims being associated with convergent eyes and side-swing captures occurring in the absence of eye convergence.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis based on the observed associations between eye movements and capture strategies.

claim: These two strategies (convergent eyes with S-strikes/attack swims vs. divergent eyes with side swings) may have been present in a common ancestor of teleosts, with one or the other becoming dominant in certain lineages.
source: These two strategies may have been present in a common ancestor of teleosts, with one or the other becoming dominant in certain lineages.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis about the ancestral state and diversification of prey capture strategies.

claim: Comparing neural circuitry across these experimentally tractable animals could help pinpoint evolvable circuit nodes ('hotspots' of evolutionary change) and genetic loci that underlie prey localization strategies and swim kinematics in fishes.
source: Comparing neural circuitry across these (now) experimentally tractable animals could help pinpoint evolvable circuit nodes ('hotspots' of evolutionary change; Roberts et al., 2022; Seeholzer et al., 2018) and genetic loci that underlie prey localization strategies and swim kinematics in fishes.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about future research directions, with citations to relevant concepts.

source: We believe that a detailed and quantitative description of behavior is an important first step toward uncovering underlying neural mechanisms and relating behavioral differences between species to their ecological niches.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' perspective on the value of their approach.

claim: The spitting behavior in L. attenuatus likely explains the high incidence of hunt initiations when prey items are already in the central visual field in this species.
source: This behavior likely explains the high incidence of hunt initiations when prey items are already in the central visual field in this species (Figure 4A, B, and D).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed spitting behavior to the prey positioning data.

evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed spitting behavior.
